catalog_quote: Black & Black (1971: 14) mention a correlation between vowel lengthening and stress in Moro: Stress presents a problem because it fluctuates freely in many words. It also seems to vary with the intonation pattern and is affected by elision. However for the most part a rough prediction can be given. 1. If the last syllable is closed, it is stressed. 2. If it is open the stress moves to the pentultimate unless this syllable contains /ə/. 3. If so the stress moves further to the front to the nearest syllable not containing /ə/, or, 4. If the word is only 2 syllable, the stress returns to the ultimate. ... It is not clear what Black & Black (1971) perceive to be stress in Moro. They did not recognize Moro to be a tone language in their grammar, and as English speakers, they may have interpreted pitch differences as stress, since high pitch is an acoustic correlate of stress in English. ... …
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Moro (moro1285) is not in the catalog. The single works with stress in the title, Jenks & Rose 2011 NLLT 'High tone in Moro', was obtained in full as an open-access PDF (via the rd.springer.com mirror; saved and logged). It is a tone paper: Moro has privative H vs. L; stress appears only comparatively (pp. 228-229: duration/intensity evidence for feet 'not strong'; p. 234: H follows a (C)VC > CV > V prominence scale 'similar to stress systems'; p. 246: verb H is 'stress-like', noun H 'tone-like'). It makes no claim about word-stress placement. The best first-hand stress statement remains the Jenks, Julima, Naser & Rose LangSci grammar sec. 2.1.14 (already held by the project, re-read): it quotes Black & Black's 1971 stress rules (closed ultima, else penult, /ə/-avoidance), argues they are likely misheard tone, reports no systematic duration-by-position effect, and leaves 'whether Moro has stress or prominence of some kind.. undetermined'. Black & Black 1971 (print only, Khartoum) is the only source asserting stress and is low priority since its stress passage is quoted in full in the grammar. Nothing here contradicts anything, since there is no catalog record; recommended coding: tone language, word stress undetermined.

new_statements.quote: It is not clear what Black & Black (1971) perceive to be stress in Moro. They did not recognize Moro to be a tone language in their grammar, and as English speakers, they may have interpreted pitch differences as stress [...] If Moro has stress, tone is not a correlate of stress. Any type of syllable (open/closed) and any type of vowel may bear either high or low tone. [...] duration does not appear to be tied to position in a systematic way. [...] We have not conducted an instrumental study to determine this, and at this point, the question of whether Moro has stress or prominence of some kind is left undetermined.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened the copy we hold (788 pp., the PDF's metadata gives the title 'A grammar of Moro', authors Jenks/Julima/Naser/Rose, created 2025-11-27; CC BY 4.0 LangSci proofreading version served openly from github.com/langsci/569 gh-pages). Sec. 2.1.14 'Vowel Length and Stress' is on printed pp. 47-48 (PDF pp. 71-72) exactly as located. Every sentence of the reported quote is present verbatim: 'It is not clear what Black & Black (1971) perceive to be stress in Moro. They did not recognize Moro to be a tone language in their grammar, and as English speakers, they may have interpreted pitch differences as stress, since high pitch is an acoustic correlate of stress in English.'.. 'If Moro has stress…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Moro is a two-tone (H vs L, privative H) language. The modern reference grammar finds no evidence for word stress: tone is independent of syllable type/position, a pilot duration study shows no systematic penult/final lengthening, and the existence of stress or any non-tonal prominence is explicitly left undetermined. The only positive stress rule in the literature is Black & Black 1971:14 (final syllable if closed, else penult unless it contains /ə/, then the nearest non-ə syllable further left; disyllables revert to final), which the grammar quotes and attributes to misheard H tone plus phrase-final lengthening.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said about secondary stress in either source.
new_statements.exceptions: Black & Black 1971 (as quoted): stress 'fluctuates freely in many words', varies with intonation and elision; vowel lengthening under stress only in isolation forms. Grammar: one of four disyllabic nouns (ðáɾá) showed a significantly longer final vowel; trisyllable durations depend on the intervening consonant, not position; phrase-final lengthening exists only in story/list intonation (sec. 4.6.4).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress is the topic; the grammar suggests B&B's lengthening reflects isolation/utterance-final (phrase-level) position rather than word-internal stress. Duration measurements were on nouns in phrase-final position of SVO carrier sentences.
new_statements.identity_note: The grammar describes the Thetogovela variety of Moro (language-level glottocode moro1285; dialect-level glottocode not verified). Black & Black 1971, whose stress rules the grammar quotes and disputes, described a different (Umm Dorein-area) variety per the grammar's framing; both are Moro [mor].

new_statements.quote: It is not clear what Black & Black (1971) perceive to be stress in Moro. They did not recognize Moro to be a tone language in their grammar, and as English speakers, they may have interpreted pitch differences as stress [...] If pitch and duration do not convey stress, other factors such as intensity, consonant production or vowel quality might be indicators of prominence. We have not conducted an instrumental study to determine this, and at this point, the question of whether Moro has stress or prominence of some kind is left undetermined.
new_statements.citation: Jenks, Peter, Elyasir Julima, Angelo Naser & Sharon Rose. Forthcoming (proofreading version 2025-11-27). A grammar of Moro (with a focus on the Thetogovela dialect). Berlin: Language Science Press (book 569). Sec. 2.1.14 'Vowel Length and Stress'.
new_statements.reading: Moro is a two-tone (privative H) language; the modern grammar explicitly declines to say whether Moro has word stress at all. The only positive stress rules (Black & Black 1971: final closed syllable, else penult, avoiding /ə/) are quoted by the grammar and dismissed as probable misperception of tone; a small duration study found no systematic positional lengthening. For catalog purposes Moro should be coded as tone language, stress undetermined/not established (no fixed-position stress claim survives). Caveat: the PDF we hold is the proofreading version with a 'Do not quote' banner; the final LangSci version should be checked before citing page numbers. The NLLT 2011 paper (this search of works with stress in the title's sole item) adds only that H in verbs is 'stress-like' in Hyman's typological sense and that phonetic evidence for feet is 'not strong' (pp. 228-229).

sources.note: Sec. 2.1.14 'Vowel Length and Stress' (pp. 47-48): no contrastive length; quotes Black & Black 1971:14-15 stress rules (final closed syllable stressed, else penult unless it has /ə/, then nearest non-ə syllable leftward; disyllables revert to final), argues B&B likely mistook H tone for stress; tone is not a correlate of stress; small duration study finds no systematic positional lengthening; concludes 'the question of whether Moro has stress or prominence of some kind is left undetermined.' Ch. 4: two tones, H vs L (privative H), H spreads/shifts/downsteps.

sources.citation: Jenks, Peter & Sharon Rose. 2011. High tone in Moro: effects of prosodic categories and morphological domains. Natural Language & Linguistic Theory 29(1): 211-250.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request); access check: open copy online
sources.quote: It would be preferable if there were independent arguments for feet, such as intensity or vowel duration, but there is a lack of clear evidence. Short verb roots typically contain a vowel that is longer than surrounding vowels: [kawáðá] 'poke', a property that is often associated with primary stress. Yet long verb roots typically contain a schwa in one of the two positions making vowel duration comparisons difficult. [...] Thus, while the duration facts are suggestive of a trochaic foot aligned with the left edge of the root, the evidence is not strong.
sources.locator: pp. 228-229 (Sect. 4.1, foot-based analysis of tone doubling); also p. 234 (Sect. 4.2) and p. 246 (conclusion)
sources.note: A tone paper (privative H vs. L, Thetogovela dialect), not a stress paper. Stress enters only comparatively: on pp. 228-229 the authors look for phonetic correlates (duration, intensity) of the bimoraic foot they use to model binary H spreading in verbs, find a longer root-initial vowel in short verb roots ('a property that is often associated with primary stress') but call the evidence 'not strong' and intensity 'inconclusive'; on p. 234 they say H distribution in D-stems follows a syllable-prominence scale (C)VC > CV > V 'similar to stress systems that show both rime and onset sensitivity';…

sources.note: H tone placement on Thetogovela Moro verb stems is weight- and onset-sensitive, analysed with a stress-like prominence scale (C)VC > CV > V and foot-bounded tone doubling; treats Moro as a privative-H tone language and makes no claim that Moro has word stress.
